'''Henry Rishbeth''' (1931–2010)<ref name = "Mendillo"/> was a British physicist with a research focus on the [[ionosphere]]. He won the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] in 2001.

==Biography==
===Early life and family===
Henry Rishbeth was born in 1931 to [[Oswald Rishbeth]], an Australian geographer, and [[Kathleen Rishbeth]], a British zoologist. Henry had two siblings, including John, a biologist. Henry's maternal grandfather was anthropologist [[Alfred Cort Haddon]], and his paternal ancestry links him with the influential Rischbieth family in Australia, including members such as [[Charles Rischbieth]], [[Henry Wills Rischbieth]], [[Bessie Rischbieth]] and [[Charles Rischbieth Jury]].<ref name = "Mendillo">Mendillo, M., "[https://cedarweb.vsp.ucar.edu/wiki/images/c/c4/2010_Rishbeth_by_Mendillo.pdf Henry Rishbeth: A remembrance] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028175649/http://cedarweb.vsp.ucar.edu/wiki/images/c/c4/2010_Rishbeth_by_Mendillo.pdf |date=28 October 2021 }}", 25th CEDAR Meeting, Boulder, CO., June 2010.</ref>

===Scientific career===
Rishbeth studied at the [[University of Cambridge]], receiving a BA (1954) MA(1958), PhD (1960) and ScD (1972). In between his BA and MA, Rishbeth was at [[CSIRO]] from 1955 to 1957.<ref name = "Mendillo"/> from 1955 to 1958, Rishbeth was mostly working in [[radio astronomy]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Interview with Henry Rishbeth |url=https://www.nrao.edu/archives/items/show/15144 |publisher=National Radio Astronomy Observatory |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref><ref name=NAM>{{cite web |title=Dr. Henry Rishbeth |url=https://corpora.tika.apache.org/base/docs/govdocs1/130/130575.html |publisher=National Astronomy Meeting, 2001 |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref> At Cambridge, he studied under [[J. A. Ratcliffe]] for his PhD before moving to the [[Radio Research Station (UK)|Radio Research Station]] in [[Slough]].<ref name=Weiss/> He briefly worked at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] as a consultant from 1962 to 1965 before returning to his previous institution in the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name=NAM/> Back in Slough, he was awarded Individual Merit Scientist in 1972 and was the deputy director from 1977 to 1979.<ref name=NAM/> in 1969, he published ''Introduction to Ionospheric Physics'' with [[Owen Garriott]]. He moved with the Radio Research Station (by then called the Appleton laboratory) to the [[Rutherford Appleton Laboratory]] in 1979 before moving to an academic position at the [[University of Southampton]]<ref name=Weiss>{{cite journal |last1=Weiss |first1=Nigel |title=Prof. Henry Rishbeth: The RAS Gold Medal 2001 Get access Arrow |journal=Astronomy & Geophysics |date=August 2002 |volume=43 |issue=4 |page=4 |doi=10.1093/astrog/43.4.4.6 |url=https://academic.oup.com/astrogeo/article-abstract/43/4/4.6/343045?redirectedFrom=fulltext |access-date=24 October 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> in 1981 as a senior visiting fellow. He was appointed visiting professor in 1990, Research Professor in 1991 and emeritus in 1996 at the university.<ref name=NAM/>

Rishbeth is particularly known for studies on the [[ionosphere]]'s [[F region|F2 region]].<ref name=Weiss/> He also did pioneering work on radio wave propagation with [[David W. Barron]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Professor David Barron 1935–2012, 'a founding father of computer science' |url=https://web-archive.southampton.ac.uk/www.ecs.soton.ac.uk-2022/www.ecs.soton.ac.uk/news/3911.html |publisher=University of Southampton |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref> Rishbeth was the first to suggest that [[global warming]] would produce a decrease in ionospheric temperature, leading to detectable effects that could provide evidence of the presence of [[climate change]].<ref name=Weiss/>

Rishbeth established the Magnetosphere Ionosphere and Solar-Terrestrial group, a physical sciences community based in the [[United Kingdom]] associated with the [[Royal Astronomical Society]], along with Peter Kendall.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rishbeth |first1=Henry |title=MIST History |url=https://www.mist.ac.uk/community/mist-history |publisher=MIST |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref> He then organised the first meetings of the group from 1970 to 1988. Rishbeth was also an important figure in the establishment of [[EISCAT]]. He also occupied positions in [[International Association of Geomagnetism and Aeronomy]],<ref name=Weiss/> the [[Royal Astronomical Society]], the [[International Union of Radio Science]], the [[International Council for Science]], and the [[International Academy of Astronautics]],<ref name=NAM/> as well as serving on the [[World Data Center|ICSU Panel on World Data Centers]].<ref name=Weiss/>

Rishbeth died in 2010. He remained active in his scientific field until his death.<ref>{{cite web |title=Special Meeting in Memory of Prof. Henry Rishbeth |url=http://www.sp.ph.ic.ac.uk/~ingomw/henry/Henry_Meeting/Welcome.html |publisher=Imperial College London |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref>

==Awards==
Rishbeth received the [[International Union of Radio Science|URSI]] [[Edward Victor Appleton|Appleton]] prize in 1981, was the 1995 [[Marcel Nicolet]] Lecturer at the [[American Geophysical Union]],<ref name=NAM/> and won the 2001 [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]]. In 2006, he won the [[Granville Beynon|Sir Granville Beynon]] medal from [[EISCAT]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Beynon Medals |url=https://eiscat.se/about/sir-granville-beynon-awards/ |publisher=EISCAT |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref> There was an award named after him which was given by the MIST body that he founded from 2005 to 2008.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Rishbeth Prize |url=https://www.mist.ac.uk/2-uncategorised/10-the-rishbeth-prize |publisher=MIST |access-date=24 October 2024}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Rishbeth was married to Priscilla Rishbeth, with whom he had two daughters.<ref name = "Mendillo"/>
